title: Decision-aware validation of zero-noise extrapolation in QAOA optimization landscapes
abstract: Zero-noise extrapolation (ZNE) is usually validated by the accuracy of mitigated observables, yet variational quantum optimization uses those observables to select parameters. We ask whether, and by how much, an accuracy gain from ZNE coincides with a worse decision. In depth-one simulations of the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) for MaxCut on four to six qubits, each sampled $120\times120$ landscape yields both its mean-squared error (MSE) and the ideal regret of its selected grid minimum, comparing Richardson orders one to three with unmitigated estimation at the same total shot budget per grid point. In an exploratory screen of 675 conditions, whose per-point random seeds collide, a familywise (Holm) analysis retains only four of 540 replication conditions as showing both directional MSE improvement and regret increase. A frozen confirmation with 100 fresh paired repetitions per condition reproduces all four: median MSE improvements of 7.65-73.09% accompany median normalized regret increases of only 0.0031-0.0073. We distinguish a bias route, in which residual bias reorders the mean landscape, from a variance route, in which Richardson weights amplify finite-shot noise. Exact first and second moments on a bounded control grid find no bias-route reversal: mitigated mean landscapes preserve the ideal minima, and ZNE can more than halve expected MSE, yet finite-shot selections incur higher mean regret. Decision losses that survive strict testing are few and small in this benchmark, but reproducible and not revealed by aggregate MSE. We present a paired benchmark and recommend reporting decision regret alongside estimation error when mitigation is assessed for optimization. Results concern simulated exhaustive grids, not hardware or optimizer loops.
summary: This work rigorously tests the assumption that reducing noise in quantum measurements via Zero-Noise Extrapolation (ZNE) automatically improves the performance of variational quantum algorithms like QAOA. The authors find that while ZNE can substantially lower estimation error (MSE), this gain does not guarantee better decision-making, as evidenced by minimal or slightly increased parameter regret.
main_problem: The paper investigates whether the accuracy gains achieved through Zero-Noise Extrapolation (ZNE) in variational quantum optimization (QAOA) correspond to a better decision, measured by parameter regret.
main_result: While ZNE can significantly reduce the Mean-Squared Error (MSE) of observables, the study finds that these improvements often accompany only negligible or slightly increased mean regret, suggesting that decision-making must be validated alongside estimation error.
method: The authors perform in-depth simulations on QAOA optimization landscapes, comparing unmitigated estimation against ZNE using Richardson orders, and quantifying performance using both MSE and normalized regret.
model_or_system: The model is the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) applied to the MaxCut problem on 4 to 6 qubits. The analysis is performed on simulated, exhaustive optimization grids.
key_observables: Mean-Squared Error (MSE) and normalized simple regret ($R$), used to assess both estimation accuracy and decision quality.
important_parameters: Depolarizing channel parameter ($p$), total shot budget ($B$), and Richardson extrapolation orders ($m=1, 2, 3$).
main_assumptions: The results are based on simulated exhaustive grids, not actual hardware or adaptive optimization loops, and the confirmation is limited to a small set of tested conditions.
figures_summary: The notes reference tables and figures showing the comparison of MSE improvements (7.65–73.09%) versus minimal regret increases (0.0031–0.0073) for the few conditions that passed rigorous statistical testing.
paper_structure: The paper follows a structure of defining the problem (ZNE vs. decision quality), developing paired metrics (MSE vs. Regret), conducting an exploratory screening analysis (Holm correction), and finally presenting a frozen confirmation on fresh data to draw conclusions.
why_interesting: It provides a crucial, rigorous benchmark for quantum algorithm developers, warning that optimizing only for low noise (low MSE) might lead to poor algorithmic performance (high regret) in practical optimization tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Paired effects in the replication family. (a) Median relative mean-squared- error improvement and median normalized regret change for the 507 eligible conditions; excluded conditions are omitted, and the four Holm rejections are shown as larger orange points. The horizontal axis uses a symmetric logarithmic scale to retain large negative relative improvements. (b) Medians and seed interquartile ranges of the regret change for the four retained conditions.

Figure 2: Bias–variance control on a 12 × 12 grid with B = 1024 shots per point for every method and 500 repetitions per configuration: exact grid-averaged squared bias and sampling variance (stacked bars) and Monte Carlo estimates of the mean-squared error with ±1.96 standard errors (points). This control is separate from the 120 × 120 screen.

Figure 3: Decision outcomes for the bias–variance control (12 × 12 grid, B = 1024, 500 repetitions per configuration): normalized ideal regret of exact-mean and finite-shot selections. A common vertical scale is used for all graphs. Error bars denote ±1.96 Monte Carlo standard errors and are descriptive.
